# From a data frame to an evidence-based explanation

This contributor-training lesson introduces the R-LearnXR pattern. Learners work with a small synthetic dataset so they can focus on the workflow: identify a row, make a prediction, run R, inspect exact coordinates, explain a claim, and reproduce the result.

::: {.callout-note}
## Learning objectives

By the end, learners can:

1. Identify `label`, `x`, `y`, and `z` as a simple scene data contract.
2. Predict what a filter or transformation will retain.
3. Use one coordinate as evidence while naming a limitation.
4. Export a reproducible source path and learning receipt.
:::

## R01 warm-up: what is one row?

Open `data/learning_points.csv` and answer: “What does one row represent, and which columns identify the observation versus its coordinates?” This is the same question used in the [R Foundations micro-lessons](../../docs/curriculum/r-foundations-micro-lessons.md).

## Make a prediction

Before running code, predict which labels will remain after a transformation that keeps points with positive `x` and negative `y`. Write the rule in plain language, not only as code.

## Run the reproducible R pipeline

```{r}
#| echo: true
source("../../R/utils.R")
source("../../R/zzz.R")
source("../../R/scene_contract.R")
source("../../R/render_scene.R")

demo <- read.csv("data/learning_points.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
set.seed(2026)
render_scene(
  demo,
  x = "x",
  y = "y",
  z = "z",
  labels = demo$label,
  output_dir = "scene",
  title = "R-LearnXR reference data space",
  overwrite = TRUE
)
summary(demo[, c("x", "y", "z")])
```

Ask learners to identify the three reproducibility decisions: the input file, the coordinate mapping, and the seed. The scene is a visual evidence layer over this ordinary R code.

[Open the interactive 3D scene](scene/index.html)

## Explore and explain

Use the 3D scene or the accessible table to select one point. Complete this sentence:

> Point ___ is ___ on the ___ axis at approximately ___, so I infer ___. This does not prove ___ because ___.

Then select a second point and compare one coordinate. The explanation should use a point, an axis, and an interpretation—not a color or visual impression alone.

## Transfer and reproduce

Change the filter rule, rerun the code, and predict how the returned rows will change. Export the R or Quarto source and inspect the receipt for prediction, explanation, selected evidence, runtime, seed, row count, and artifact hash.

## Teaching support

Use this lesson before the [Penguin PCA flagship lesson](../penguin-pca/index.qmd). For the full statistics pathway, see [statistics modules](../../docs/curriculum/statistics-modules.md) and [R foundations micro-lessons](../../docs/curriculum/r-foundations-micro-lessons.md).

The browser scene is not dependent on a headset. A future version may expose WebXR when a compatible device is available.
